rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem:
Out of \(\mathrm{Ti^{3+}}\), \(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}\), \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) and \(\mathrm{Ni^{2+}}\) ions, the one which is the most stable ion in aqueous solution is :
[Atomic number : Ti = 22, Cr = 24, Fe = 26, Ni = 28]
rows.solution:
Stability in aqueous solution goes with a specially favourable d configuration, and among these four only one has it. \(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}\) is \(3d^3\): in an octahedral aqua complex those three electrons occupy the three \(t_{2g}\) orbitals singly, giving an exactly half-filled lower set — an arrangement of considerable extra stability, and the reason chromium(III) is the dominant oxidation state of chromium in solution.

The others are all less settled. \(\mathrm{Ti^{3+}}\) is \(3d^1\) and is readily oxidised to the \(d^0\) \(\mathrm{Ti^{4+}}\). \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) is \(3d^6\) and is oxidised in air to \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}\), which is the half-filled \(3d^5\). \(\mathrm{Ni^{2+}}\) is \(3d^8\) and stable enough, but without the half-filled advantage.

rows.stem: Hoffmann Bromamide degradation reaction is given by :
rows.solution:
Hofmann bromamide degradation converts an AMIDE into a primary amine with one carbon fewer, using bromine in aqueous alkali:
\(\mathrm{R-CONH_2} + \mathrm{Br_2} + 4\mathrm{NaOH} \longrightarrow \mathrm{R-NH_2} + \mathrm{Na_2CO_3} + 2\mathrm{NaBr} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}\)
So the compound that GIVES the reaction is \(\mathrm{R-CO-NH_2}\). \(\mathrm{R-NH_2}\) is its product rather than its substrate; a nitro compound is reduced, not degraded; and \(\mathrm{R-CH_2-NH_2}\) is already an amine.

rows.stem: Out of the following statements, the correct statement is :

options.label: A
options.text: La is actually not an element of transition series.

options.label: B
options.text: Zr and Hf have almost identical atomic radii.

rows.solution:
Only one of the four statements is correct. Zirconium and hafnium DO have almost identical atomic radii, because lanthanoid contraction across the intervening f-block cancels the increase that the extra period would otherwise bring — which is why the two are notoriously hard to separate.

Of the others: lanthanum IS an element of the transition series, \([\mathrm{Xe}]5d^1 6s^2\); the lanthanoids are NOT radioactive, apart from promethium — it is the actinoids that are radioactive throughout; and the ionic radius DECREASES from \(\mathrm{La^{3+}}\) to \(\mathrm{Lu^{3+}}\), which is what lanthanoid contraction means.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem: Which of the following properties of transition metals enables them to behave as catalysts ?
rows.solution:
VARIABLE OXIDATION STATES. A catalyst works by offering a lower-energy path, and a transition metal does that by accepting electrons from one reactant and passing them to another — moving between oxidation states and returning to its original state at the end. Iron in the Haber process and vanadium(V) oxide in the Contact process both work this way.

High melting point, high ionisation enthalpy and alloy formation are all genuine properties of transition metals, but none of them supplies a reaction path. (The other real catalytic mechanism, adsorption of reactants on the metal surface through vacant d orbitals, is not among the options.)

rows.stem: What amount of electric charge is required for the oxidation of 1 mole of FeO to \(\mathrm{Fe_2O_3}\) ?
rows.solution:
Work from the change in oxidation state, not from formula masses. In FeO iron is \(+2\); in \(\mathrm{Fe_2O_3}\) it is \(+3\). Each iron atom therefore loses exactly ONE electron, so 1 mol of FeO requires 1 mol of electrons:
\(Q = 1 \times F = 96500\ \mathrm{C}\), that is 1 F.

The trap is the subscript 2 in \(\mathrm{Fe_2O_3}\), which tempts a factor of 2; but the question asks about one mole of FeO, and that contains one mole of iron.

rows.stem: Name and define the cell which was used for providing electric power in the Apollo space programme. Also write its one advantage.
rows.solution:
The cell used in the Apollo space programme was the HYDROGEN-OXYGEN FUEL CELL.

A fuel cell is a galvanic cell in which the energy of combustion of a fuel — here hydrogen — is converted DIRECTLY into electrical energy, the reactants being supplied continuously from outside rather than stored within the cell.

One advantage: it has a high efficiency, around 70%, because the chemical energy goes straight to electricity instead of passing through heat, so it is not limited by the Carnot efficiency of a heat engine. It is also pollution free, its only product being water — which on Apollo was drunk by the crew.

rows.stem: \(\mathrm{PdCl_2 \cdot 2KCl}\) does not give precipitate of AgCl with \(\mathrm{AgNO_3}\) solution. Write the structural formula and IUPAC name of the complex.
rows.solution:
No precipitate with silver nitrate means no free chloride in solution, so BOTH chlorides must lie inside the coordination sphere and the two potassium ions are the counter ions.

Structural formula: \(\mathrm{K_2[PdCl_4]}\)

Four chlorido ligands contribute \(-4\) and the two potassium ions \(+2\), so palladium is \(+2\). The complex is the anion, so palladium takes the \(-ate\) ending.

IUPAC name: potassium tetrachloridopalladate(II)

rows.subtopic: Factors Influencing Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem:
The reaction between \(\mathrm{A_2\,(g)}\) and \(\mathrm{B_2\,(g)}\) was carried out in a sealed isothermal container. The rate law for the reaction was found to be :
\(\mathrm{Rate = k[A_2]\,[B_2]}\)
If 1 mole of \(\mathrm{A_2\,(g)}\) was added to the reaction chamber and the temperature was kept constant, then predict the change in rate of the reaction and the rate constant.
rows.solution:
Adding 1 mole of \(\mathrm{A_2}\) to a sealed container of fixed volume raises \([\mathrm{A_2}]\). Since the rate law is \(\text{Rate} = k[\mathrm{A_2}][\mathrm{B_2}]\), the RATE OF THE REACTION INCREASES in proportion to that rise.

The RATE CONSTANT REMAINS THE SAME. By the Arrhenius equation \(k = Ae^{-E_a/RT}\), the constant depends only on the temperature and on the nature of the reaction — not on how much of anything is present — and the temperature was held constant. Concentration moves the rate; only temperature moves the constant.

rows.stem:
Reactant ‘A’ underwent a decomposition reaction. The concentration of ‘A’ was measured periodically and recorded in the table given below :

| Time / Hours | [A]/M |
|---|---|
| 0 | \(0{\cdot}88\) |
| 1 | \(0{\cdot}44\) |
| 2 | \(0{\cdot}22\) |
| 3 | \(0{\cdot}11\) |

Based on the above data, predict the order of the reaction and write the expression for the rate law.
rows.solution:
Read the table for a pattern rather than fitting an equation. The concentration halves in each successive hour: 0.88 to 0.44, 0.44 to 0.22, 0.22 to 0.11. The HALF-LIFE is therefore constant at 1 hour, whatever concentration it starts from.

A half-life independent of the starting concentration is the signature of a FIRST order reaction, for which \(t_{1/2} = 0.693/k\) contains no concentration term at all. For any other order the half-life would change as the reaction proceeded.

Order of the reaction: 1 (first order)
Rate law: \(\text{Rate} = k[\mathrm{A}]\)

rows.stem:
(a) Can sodium propoxide and t-butyl chloride be used for the preparation of t-butyl propyl ether ? Give suitable explanation. Justify your answer by suggesting the appropriate starting material required for the preparation of t-butyl propyl ether.
(b) Give the IUPAC name of the above mentioned ether.
rows.solution:
(a) No, that pairing cannot be used.

Williamson synthesis is an \(\mathrm{S_N}2\) reaction, so the alkoxide must attack a LESS hindered carbon. Sodium propoxide is a strong nucleophile but also a strong BASE, and t-butyl chloride's carbon is fully substituted and inaccessible to attack from behind. Instead of substituting, the propoxide removes a \(\beta\) hydrogen and eliminates, giving 2-methylpropene rather than the ether.

Reversing the roles solves it: use PROPYL CHLORIDE as the halide and SODIUM tert-BUTOXIDE as the alkoxide, so the alkoxide attacks a primary carbon where \(\mathrm{S_N}2\) works cleanly.
\((\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{C-ONa} + \mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2Cl} \longrightarrow (\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{C-O-CH_2CH_2CH_3} + \mathrm{NaCl}\)

(b) The parent chain is propane with a methyl and a propoxy group on C-2:
2-propoxy-2-methylpropane

rows.stem:
An aqueous solution of NaOH was made and its molar mass from the measurement of osmotic pressure at \(25^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) was found to be 28 g \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\). Calculate the percentage dissociation of NaOH in this solution.
[Atomic mass : Na = \(23{\cdot}0\) u, O = \(16{\cdot}0\) u, H = \(1{\cdot}0\) u]
rows.solution:
The van't Hoff factor is the ratio of the normal molar mass to the abnormal one:
\(i = \dfrac{\text{normal molar mass}}{\text{abnormal molar mass}}\)

Sodium hydroxide has \(M = 23.0 + 16.0 + 1.0 = 40\) g \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\), and the measurement gave 28 g \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\):
\(i = \dfrac{40}{28} = 1.428\)

For dissociation into \(n\) particles, \(\alpha = \dfrac{i-1}{n-1}\), and sodium hydroxide gives two ions, so \(n = 2\):
\(\alpha = \dfrac{1.428 - 1}{2 - 1} = 0.428\)

The percentage dissociation is \(0.428 \times 100 = 42.8\%\).

The abnormal molar mass came out LOWER than the true one, which is the signature of dissociation: more particles than the formula suggests means a larger colligative property and a smaller apparent mass.

rows.stem:
Calculate the cell voltage of the voltaic cell which is set up by joining the following half-cells at \(25^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\).
\(\mathrm{Al/Al^{3+}}\) \((0{\cdot}002\ \mathrm{M})\) and \(\mathrm{Ni/Ni^{2+}}\) \((0{\cdot}002\ \mathrm{M})\)
Given : \(\mathrm{E^{o}_{Ni^{2+}/Ni}} = -\,0{\cdot}25\) V
\(\mathrm{E^{o}_{Al^{3+}/Al}} = -\,1{\cdot}66\) V
\(\log 5 = 0{\cdot}6990\)
rows.solution:
Aluminium has the more negative potential, so it is the anode and nickel the cathode:
\(E^{\circ}_{cell} = E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Ni^{2+}/Ni}} - E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Al^{3+}/Al}} = (-0.25) - (-1.66) = 1.41\ \mathrm{V}\)

Balancing electrons gives \(2\mathrm{Al} + 3\mathrm{Ni^{2+}} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{Al^{3+}} + 3\mathrm{Ni}\), so \(n = 6\):
\(E_{cell} = E^{\circ}_{cell} - \dfrac{0.059}{6}\log\dfrac{[\mathrm{Al^{3+}}]^2}{[\mathrm{Ni^{2+}}]^3}\)
\(= 1.41 - \dfrac{0.059}{6}\log\dfrac{(2 \times 10^{-3})^2}{(2 \times 10^{-3})^3}\)

With both concentrations equal the quotient collapses to the reciprocal of one of them:
\(\dfrac{(2 \times 10^{-3})^2}{(2 \times 10^{-3})^3} = \dfrac{1}{2 \times 10^{-3}} = 5 \times 10^{2}\)

so the logarithm is \(\log 5 + 2 = 0.6990 + 2 = 2.6990\), which is what the supplied \(\log 5\) is for:
\(E_{cell} = 1.41 - \dfrac{0.059}{6}(2.6990) = 1.41 - 0.0265\)
\(E_{cell} = 1.3835\ \mathrm{V}\)
